Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
I try to erase the memory of the event
I think about why the event has happened to me

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner, being triggered by male presence and related people is coherent, but explosion/bang sounds points toward combat, accidents, or blast-related trauma and is hard to reconcile as a core trigger here without any matching assault-context cue elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile reflects fear, avoidance, hypervigilance, fragmented memory, and negative self/world appraisals. Endorsing risky behavior pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported by other selected items; it reads as a different coping/symptom pattern than the otherwise strongly avoidant-threat profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: A marked loss of connection to community and culture is not well anchored to the rest of this intimate-partner-violence profile. The other appraisals center on danger, contamination, and shattered beliefs, but nothing else suggests cultural/community rupture, making this item feel clinically disconnected rather than tightly linked to the stated trauma formulation.

vignette: Clara Vance had spent forty years trying to arrange the fragments of that winter into a sequence that made sense, but the moments refused to line up. They remained as sharp, disconnected pictures: the heavy oak door of their apartment hurling shut, the sudden impact against her shoulder, the way her former partner’s face had shifted from familiar to unrecognizable in a single breath. At the time, the violence had been confined to their home, a place where the slamming of doors had once signaled the end of an evening together, or the beginning of a sudden, breathless panic when the exits became irrelevant. Now, those same sounds carried the weight of that original shock. She had come to believe that the world no longer operated by predictable rules. The trust she had once placed in how people were meant to behave had splintered, leaving her certain that those around her could never be relied upon. In the months that followed, her nights grew heavy. She began associating late afternoons with the approaching dark, knowing those hours were the ones that invited dreams she refused to entertain. Instead of resting, she would sit by the window until her eyes burned, then rise to check every door and window in her house. When she finally did drift off, fragments of the past would surface without warning: a snapshot of a raised hand, the blur of a slamming door, the cold floor against her cheek. Each image was followed by a wave of grief so heavy it left her gasping. She tried to erase the memory of the event, willing it to dissolve, but it only grew heavier. During the day, her body remained wound tight, every sound pulling her attention to the edges of the room. She was superalert, watching the periphery, and she learned to position herself facing any entrance as soon as she walked into a space. Her work as a social worker became a landscape of careful navigation. At the county clinic where she had spent decades supporting families, she adjusted her practice to fit the architecture of her alertness. She avoided being alone with men, insisting on open-door policies or having a colleague present, and she stepped back from cases involving known people and related people, recognizing that familiar faces carried the same unpredictable weight as strangers. When a client’s chair scraped against the linoleum or a heavy file cabinet door snapped shut, her breath would catch, and her eyes would drift to the exit before she could force herself to speak. The physical toll mounted; her bed remained cool, and the feeling of contamination clung to her skin no matter how often she washed. She found herself asking the same quiet question over and over, thinking about why the event had happened to her. The routine of the clinic, once a source of steady purpose, now demanded constant vigilance, and she had learned to navigate the fluorescent-lit corridors with measured steps, always aware of who stood nearby and what sounds might suddenly echo down the hall. At eighty, Clara’s hands tremble not from age, but from the relentless watchfulness that has become her constant companion. What finally brought her to this intake office was not a single breaking point, but the quiet exhaustion of carrying a shattered worldview alone. She had come to believe that the foundations she once held—the safety of home, the reliability of love, the basic decency of strangers—had been completely destroyed. In this room, she sits with her back to the wall, her gaze already tracking the emergency exit, her posture braced for a sound that never comes. She does not know if the grief can ever be carried without tearing her apart, or if the dirt she feels on her hands will ever wash clean, but she knows she can no longer keep the door to her own life shut against the help she is hoping to find.
